levels.title: Concentration & Form Recognition
levels.description: Recognize the critical differences between concentrated and dilute formulation names in dispensing scenarios.
levels.learningObjective: Identify safety risks when standard drug names share identical chemical roots but differing concentrations.

activities.learningObjective: Recognize the correct product label in a surgical irrigation context to avoid dangerous concentrated glacial acid exposure.

questions.scenario: A surgical order arrives requesting dilute acetic acid for sterile surgical irrigation. The pharmacy compounding area also stores concentrated glacial acetic acid.
questions.prompt: Which medication label matches the surgical irrigation order and avoids dispensing dangerous concentrated glacial acetic acid?
questions.explanation: Acetic acid for irrigation is a dilute, non-corrosive solution. It must never be confused with glacial acetic acid, which is concentrated and causes severe chemical burns.

levels.title: Release Mechanism Discrimination
levels.description: Differentiate modified-release suffixes and distinct dosage delivery kinetics.
levels.learningObjective: Distinguish immediate-release from extended-release formulations in prescription verification.

activities.learningObjective: Differentiate immediate-release and extended-release product names during prescription verification.

questions.scenario: An outpatient prescription specifies immediate-release Adderall tablets. On the dispensary shelf, bottles for both immediate-release and extended-release formulations are stored side by side.
questions.prompt: Which product name matches the requested immediate-release prescription?
questions.explanation: Adderall designates the immediate-release formulation, whereas Adderall XR designates the extended-release formulation. Verifying the suffix prevents dosing frequency errors.

levels.title: Formulation & Suffix Distinction
levels.description: Differentiate antidiabetic and release mechanism look-alikes in dispensing contexts.
levels.learningObjective: Accurately differentiate confusable formulation pairs and sulfonylurea look-alikes.

activities.learningObjective: Identify the requested antidiabetic drug name when presented with look-alike sulfonylurea and carbonic anhydrase pairs.

questions.scenario: A patient requests a prescription refill for their oral diabetes medication, acetohexamide. Two easily confused look-alike names appear in the pharmacy computer inventory.
questions.prompt: Which medication name matches the patient's request and properly identifies the target medication?
questions.explanation: acetoHEXAMIDE is the antidiabetic sulfonylurea, distinguished by HEXAMIDE from acetaZOLAMIDE.

questions.prompt: When distinguishing Adderall formulations, which naming modifier specifically designates the extended-release product?
questions.explanation: Adderall XR uses the 'XR' (Extended Release) designation. Dispensing it in place of standard Adderall can cause dangerous dosing intervals.

levels.title: Unit 2 Mastery
levels.description: Comprehensive review and unassisted Tall Man lettering mastery for Unit 2.
levels.learningObjective: Demonstrate complete unit mastery of formulation discrimination and unassisted Tall Man lettering without prompts or scaffolding.

activities.learningObjective: Verify look-alike formulation safety under unit review conditions.

questions.scenario: A hospital order arrives for sterile wound cleansing. The medication room contains concentrated glacial acetic acid and dilute acetic acid for irrigation.
questions.prompt: Which preparation is safe for direct patient wound irrigation?
questions.explanation: Only dilute acetic acid for irrigation is safe for topical patient use; glacial acetic acid causes severe caustic burns.

activities.learningObjective: Independently produce the exact Tall Man lettering for acetohexamide without scaffolding.

questions.prompt: UNIT MASTERY CAPSTONE TASK: Type the complete drug name using correct Tall Man lettering (capitalizing the specific distinguishing letters):
questions.explanation: acetoHEXAMIDE capitalizes HEXAMIDE to emphasize the difference from acetaZOLAMIDE, which capitalizes ZOLAMIDE.
